newsitem.title: UK: GROBBELAAR DENIES GUILT IN UK SOCCER-RIGGING CASE.
newsitem.headline: GROBBELAAR DENIES GUILT IN UK SOCCER-RIGGING CASE.

text.p: Former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar on Thursday admitted in Britain's match-fixing trial that he had taken money for forecasting soccer matches but denied trying to rig games.
Zimbabwean-born Grobbelaar told a court in Winchester, southern England, that he had been paid for predicting the outcome of games by Malaysian businessman Hang Suan Lim.
"Did it ever move beyond forecasting?" Grobbelaar's lawyer Rodney Klevan asked him.
"No, forecasting was the topic of the matter," he replied.
Klevan asked: "Did you ever believe in any way that you were doing anything improper?"
Grobbelaar, 39, is accused with former Wimbledon goalkeeper Hans Segers, former Aston Villa and Wimbledon striker John Fashanu, and Lim of rigging soccer games for a Far Eastern gambling syndicate.
All defendants deny the charges, but Dutch-born Segers said he gave forecasts of Dutch games to Lim for his gambling friends in Indonesia, plus information about English teams.
It was the first time in the 21-day trial that Grobbelaar had taken the stand. Saying he had always wanted to play for Liverpool, the player said he retained his love for the team.
"It will never leave me. It is as strong today as when I first signed," he told Winchester Crown Court.
"It was a club steeped in history. There were memorable periods before I even joined them, and fantastic periods when I was with them."
It was not just a matter of football and earning a wage.
"No, it is not. It is a dream come true," he said.
Grobbelaar is the third and last of the four defendants to give evidence in the trial.
Lim and Segers have told the court money was paid for helping forecasting the results of games but not fixing matches.
Fashanu has exercised his right to silence.
